outcome: Since 26 January 2024 no exact value of the maximum snake length has been established for any dimension n of 9 or more, but lower bounds have risen for n = 9 to 13 (a July 2026 census preprint: 191, 379, 746, 1476, 2924) and for n = 13 to 20 and every d of 21 or more (a September 2026 single-author preprint), with further preprints and blog posts reporting partly superseded lengths.
problem_asks: (1) For each dimension n (n = 1, 2, 3, ...), the exact maximum length a(n) of an induced path (a snake) in the hypercube graph Q_n: a path whose non-consecutive vertices are not adjacent. Read as stated, this is one question per n, asking for the value, not for bounds or asymptotics. (2) The bullet does not fix a counting convention. Length may be counted as edges or as vertices, which differ by one. These records follow OEIS A099155 and the census and Taylor papers in counting edges. (3) Not asked by the bullet: coils (induced cycles, the sister problem), spread-k variants, or the asymptotic growth of a(n). Those are recorded below only as neighbouring work. Before the window, a(n) was known exactly for n = 1 to 8 (1, 2, 4, 7, 13, 26, 50, 98). The open cases are every n of 9 or more; n = 9 is the lowest open dimension.

events.what_happened: Ed Wynn, 'Constructing circuit codes by permuting initial sequences', arXiv 1201.1647 (submitted 8 January 2012, single version). The abstract (read) gives two constructions for coils and snakes in the hypercube, with improvements on the best known snake-in-the-box coils in dimensions 9, 10 and 11, and on other circuit codes in dimensions 8 to 13. The abstract does not state a snake of length 190 in Q9. The census (v3, Table 1) credits the previous Q9 record of 190 to Wynn [8]. I did not read the body, so that link is unverified.
events.delivers: Coil lower bounds in n = 9 to 11 and circuit-code bounds in n = 8 to 13 (abstract). The 190 snake in Q9 is attributed to this paper only by the census's citation.
events.remains: All of problem_asks for n of 9 or more.
events.directly_checkable: Finite paths in Q_n are checkable by computer. The body was not read.
events.doubts: The census's attribution of the Q9 record of 190 to this paper is not visible in the abstract.
events.direction: Lower bounds for coils and circuit codes; for snakes, the census attributes the Q9 bound of 190 to it.

events.what_happened: D. A. Casella and W. D. Potter, 'New Lower Bounds for the Snake-in-the-Box Problem: Using Evolutionary Techniques to Hunt for Snakes', FLAIRS 2005, pp. 264-269 (AAAI PDF; not opened, known from a search listing and secondary summaries). A population-based stochastic hill-climber gives new snake lower bounds for n = 9 to 12 and coil lower bounds for n = 9 to 11. A longer 2005 Casella master's thesis at the University of Georgia covers the same results.
events.delivers: Lower bounds for snakes in n = 9 to 12 (values not read).
events.remains: All of problem_asks for n of 9 or more; no exact values.
events.directly_checkable: Snakes of the reported lengths are finite paths in Q_n. The paper was not opened.
events.doubts: Classical evolutionary search. Values not read.
events.direction: Lower bounds only.
events.object: Snakes of the reported lengths in Q9 to Q12 found by stochastic hill-climbing (not read).

events.what_happened: A snake of length 98 in Q8, found by B. Carlson and confirmed by W. D. Potter. The OEIS A099155 comments (read) record Potter's February 2009 report and a note that the length was known as of December 2009. Carlson and D. Hougen later described related genetic-algorithm methods at GECCO 2010, pp. 791-798 (search listing; not opened).
events.revisions: OEIS comments dated February 2009 and a December 2009 note (read). The GECCO 2010 paper followed (not opened).
events.delivers: A lower bound a(8) of at least 98 (the value was later shown exact; see the Östergård-Pettersson event).
events.remains: All of problem_asks for n of 9 or more.
events.directly_checkable: The snake is a finite path in Q8 that can be checked by computer. The snake itself was not read.
events.direction: Lower bound at n = 8. Consistent with the exact value 98.
events.object: A 98-length snake in Q8, found by computer search (genetic-algorithm methods according to the GECCO paper's title, not read).

events.what_happened: D. Kinny, 'Monte-Carlo Search for Snakes and Coils', Springer chapter in a 2012 volume on multi-disciplinary trends in artificial intelligence (search listing; not opened). Reports that a Monte-Carlo method finds improved snake and coil solutions, faster than evolutionary methods and without tuning. A related 'A New Approach to the Snake-In-The-Box Problem' is described as Monte-Carlo-tree-search-based, but I saw it only in a search summary.

events.remains: All of problem_asks for n of 9 or more.

events.what_happened: P. R. J. Östergård and V. H. Pettersson, 'Exhaustive search for snake-in-the-box codes', Graphs and Combinatorics 31(4), 1019-1028 (DOI 10.1007/s00373-014-1423-3; the DOI suggests 2014 online and the issue is 2015). The paper is not opened. By exhaustive search with canonical augmentation it shows the maximum snake length in Q8 is 98, correcting a conjecture of 97 by Rajan and Shende. OEIS A099155 (read) credits the result to Östergård and Pettersson (2014) and records a Sloane editorial note from April 2014.
events.revisions: Published in Graphs and Combinatorics 31(4), 2015 (issue date).
events.delivers: Exact value a(8) = 98. This closes n = 8 completely. It settles nothing for n of 9 or more.
events.remains: a(n) for every n of 9 or more.

events.what_happened: S. Hood, D. Recoskie, J. Sawada and D. Wong, 'Snakes, coils, and single-track circuit codes with spread k', J. Combin. Optim. 30 (2015) 42-62 (search summary; not opened). Generalises snakes and coils with a spread k: vertices at path distance at least k must be at cube distance at least k. Reports 21 new longest k-snakes and 13 new longest k-coils, some verified optimal. The summary does not say which k the new records are for.

events.what_happened: H. L. Abbott and M. Katchalski, 'On the construction of snake in the box codes', Utilitas Mathematica 40 (1991) 97-116 (cited; not opened). Per a search summary of Allison and Paulusma's table, they gave the best known snake lower bounds for n = 14 to 20 (4932, 9866, 19738, 39478 for n = 14 to 17). They also gave the coil lower bound 77/256 times 2^n for n of 21 or more, as summarised by Taylor (2026).

events.what_happened: G. Zémor, Combinatorica 17(2) (1997): an upper bound on the length of circuit codes (coils), with a leading term of 2^(n-1). Taken from a search snippet of the combinatorial Gray codes survey (arXiv 2202.01280), not opened. The survey gives it as c(n) at most 1 + 2^(n-1) times 6n over (6n + (1/(6 sqrt 6)) sqrt n - 7). The survey notes that the coil bound does not transfer directly to snakes.
events.delivers: An upper bound for coils (the sister problem), roughly 2^(n-1) times (1 - sqrt(n)/89). It is not an upper bound for snakes as such.
events.remains: The exact snake value for every n of 9 or more.
events.doubts: Neighbouring question (coils). Recorded because it bounds the closed-path analogue.
events.direction: Upper bound on the coil problem, which is not the question asked.

events.what_happened: Hao Huang, 'Induced subgraphs of hypercubes and a proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture', arXiv 1907.00847 (2019); Annals of Mathematics 190(3), 949-955 (2019). Any induced subgraph of Q_n on more than half of its vertices has a vertex of degree at least sqrt(n). Known from search summaries and the Annals listing (not opened). It is a neighbouring theorem, not about snakes.
events.delivers: Does not itself bound snake length. Taylor (2026) uses it with the fact that a snake has maximum degree 2 to get a(d) at most 2^(d-1) - 1 for d of 5 or more (an event recorded below).
events.remains: The snake problem entirely.

events.what_happened: Federico Fuidio, Eduardo Canale and Rafael Sotelo, 'QUBO formulation for the Snake-in-the-box and Coil-in-the-box problems', arXiv 2409.04476 (submitted 5 September 2024; v1 only; abstract read). A peer-reviewed version appeared as 'QUBO Formulations for Some Graph-Theory Problems: Snake-In-The-Box and Coil-In-The-Box', IEEE QCE 2025, pp. 48-57, DOI 10.1109/QCE65121.2025.00016 (search listing; not opened).

events.delivers: A solver formulation. It reaches values only for n up to 5, which were already known exactly. It establishes no new length and moves no bound on a(n).

events.what_happened: William Echols, personal project blog post 'Lengthening hypercube snakes with windowed rerouting' (williamechols.com; page shows 'Last updated June 29, 2026' and a 1 July 2026 update; first posting date not shown). Reports coil results at n = 10 to 13, and a July 1 update that cites unpublished coils by Tom Ace of 1442 (n = 12) and 2832 (n = 13). Method: random endpoints, DFS for a longer reroute, Warnsdorff ordering. The post says the 13-dimensional snake 'matches the best known length at the time of writing' and that the 12-dimensional snake (1463) is below Ace's 1465.

events.what_happened: Paul Orland, Lucas Fagan, Michele Tarquini, Davide Passaro, Maksymilian Manko, Elli Heyes, Angus Gruen, Giorgi Butbaia, Justin Tan and Sergei Gukov, arXiv 2607.15270. First posted 16 July 2026 (v1, 5 pages) as 'A Census of New Snake-in-the-Box Records'. v1 (read through a summarising fetch) claims snakes longer than the previous best in every dimension 9 to 13. At n = 9 it states 'we find 131 distinct snakes of length 191', and says all record paths are in a 'computer-verifiable dataset'. v2 (20 July 2026) reads as v1 in the parts I could check. v3 (30 September 2026) is retitled 'New Snake-in-the-Box Records via Snakepit Surgery and Learned Construction'. It adds the Beam Anchor learned constructor, snakepits, a Snakepit-in-the-Box benchmark, and a 'Use of Large Language Models' statement. v3 Table 1 gives n = 9: 191 (previous 190); n = 10: 379 (376); n = 11: 746 (737); n = 12: 1476 (1465); n = 13: 2924 (2900). A footnote in v3 cites later reports listing 750, 1480 and 2934 for n = 11 to 13.
events.revisions: v2 20 July 2026. v3 30 September 2026: retitled; adds Beam Anchor (§5.2, App. A), snakepits, the Snakepit benchmark, and the LLM-use statement; §6 attributes the 191 to 'cube-surgery annealing alone' and the 2924 to annealing from a 2921 seed. The AI content in this event dates from v3, not v1.
events.delivers: Lower bounds only: a(9) at least 191 (previous 190); a(10) at least 379; a(11) at least 746; a(12) at least 1476; a(13) at least 2924 (v3 table). No exact value and no upper bound. v1's stated 131 symmetry classes of 191-snakes are a computational finding, with the authors conjecturing there are no others. Restricted to n = 9 to 13.
events.remains: The exact a(n) for every n of 9 or more, including whether a(9) = 191; n = 9 is still stated as open. Upper bounds are not addressed.

machine_checked.system: Computer verification as described by the authors ('computer-verifiable dataset'). The verifier was not identified in what I read.

events.directly_checkable: The 191-snake in Q9 is an explicit induced path of 191 edges (192 vertices). The paper gives one example in §3. Checking needs only the induced-path condition on the stated sequence. I did not run any check. The repository URL was not captured.
events.doubts: (a) Preprint; no review found. (b) v1 and v2 contain no learned constructor and no AI-use statement; v3 does. The v1 text gives no method for the 191 record beyond the authors' own computation. (c) The 'previous best' values conflict with later citations: v3's own footnote lists 2934 at n = 13; Taylor (23 September 2026) cites an earlier 2934 from Itty; v3's Table 1 uses 2900. (d) The v3 record provenance credits the 191 to annealing alone, while the abstract's 'Learned Construction' is not credited with any record.
events.direction: Cuts toward longer snakes: raises lower bounds at n = 9 to 13. It does not touch exact values or upper bounds, and the paper keeps n = 9 open.
events.object: An explicit snake of length 191 in Q9 (131 symmetry classes found by annealing; §3 gives one), and explicit snakes of lengths 379, 746, 1476 and 2924 in Q10 to Q13 (v3 Table 1). Constructed by computer search with data in the authors' repository.

systems.name: Beam Anchor
systems.what_it_did: A search-supervised learned constructor: a graph neural network policy on the hypercube (six residual GIN layers, width 64, per a summary of §5.2 and App. A.4). Trained from random initialisation by policy-only expert iteration, with a PPO baseline. In Q9 it finds 100 inequivalent snakes of length 190. The paper says all 100 also occur in the 1,042 length-190 classes the authors' annealer produced. §6 credits the 191 record to cube-surgery annealing alone, and no record is credited to Beam Anchor. The paper says these snakes 'substantially enlarge the published landscape at the previous record length'.
systems.basis_quote: In Q9, Beam Anchor finds 100 inequivalent snakes of length 190.

ai.disclosed_cost: From a summary of Appendix A: training ran for 12 hours on an eight-device MI250 node, and Beam Anchor first reached length 190 in Q9 after about 8 and 8.5 hours. Compute acknowledgements: Google TPU Research Cloud, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program, Nebius, and the AMD AI & HPC Cluster. The v3 text also says 'We used large language models to help structure, draft, and revise the manuscript' and 'We also used LLMs to help write and optimize code implementing the search methods and running experiments'. These name no model and are writing and coding support, so they are not listed under systems.

events.what_happened: Tom Taylor (single author), 'Constructing longer snakes and improved asymptotic bounds in hypercubes', arXiv 2609.27483 (math.CO; v1 posted 23 September 2026; read via the HTML v1 through a summarising fetch). Gives explicit snakes longer than the previous best for n = 13 to 20. Table 1: 2938, 5844, 11673, 23318, 46576, 92989, 185903, 371711 edges, against earlier values 2934, 5750, 11249, 21411, 40835, 78958, 157898, 315798. Proves a(d) at least (17/48) times 2^d for every d of 21 or more (Theorem 1). Method: twenty compatible induced paths in Q20 placed in layers of a larger cube by a binary reflected Gray code, with controlled overlaps. Base paths: Itty for Q13 and Bernatonis for Q14 to Q17, extended from an Orland et al. seed. The paper also states a(d) at most 2^(d-1) - 1 for d of 5 or more, from Huang's theorem and the fact that a snake has maximum degree 2. For d = 20 the snake is about 70.9 per cent of the upper bound 524,287, so the optimum is not known.
events.delivers: Lower bounds only: n = 13 at least 2938; n = 14 at least 5844; n = 15 at least 11673; n = 16 at least 23318; n = 17 at least 46576; n = 18 at least 92989; n = 19 at least 185903; n = 20 at least 371711; and a(d) at least (17/48) times 2^d for every d of 21 or more. Also a(d) at most 2^(d-1) - 1 for d of 5 or more (via Huang). Restricted to n = 13 to 20 and d of 21 or more. n = 9 to 12 are not addressed.
events.remains: The exact a(n) for every n of 9 or more. The optimum at n = 13 to 20 and d of 21 or more is unknown.

Its earlier n = 13 value of 2934 (from Itty) conflicts with the census's 'previous best' of 2900. The d of 21 or more bound depends on a lemma I did not check.
events.direction: Cuts toward longer snakes at n = 13 to 20 and gives an asymptotic lower bound for d of 21 or more. The Huang-based upper bound is weak in comparison with the coil bound of Zémor (1997), which is not about snakes.
events.object: Explicit snakes of 2938 edges in Q13 up to 371711 edges in Q20, from the repository. For every d of 21 or more, a construction of induced paths from twenty compatible Q20 paths joined through the layers of a larger cube, with controlled overlaps, giving (17/48) times 2^d.

disputes.summary: The n = 13 snake record is inconsistent across sources. Census v3 Table 1 gives 2924 against a previous best of 2900. Its footnote lists 2934 from later reports. Taylor (23 Sep 2026) gives 2938 as new, against an earlier 2934 from Itty. Wikipedia (retrieved 23 Jul 2026) gives 2932, citing minortriad. The undated minortriad table lists 2946. Echols gives 2898 then 2900. Ace's priming record gives 2892 in v1.

Whether the census's claim to beat the previous best in every dimension 9 to 13 holds at n = 13 depends on the date of Itty's 2934 path, which I could not locate. Taylor treats 2934 as earlier than his own 2938, while the census uses 2900 as its 'previous best'.

Values at n = 11 and n = 12 also disagree. n = 11: 732 (Ace Nov 2025), 733 or 736 (Ace Dec 2025), 737 (census 'previous'), 746 (census v3 and Wikipedia), 747 (Ace priming v2), 750 (minortriad, undated). n = 12: 1439 or 1445 (Ace), 1461 (Ace priming v1), 1463 (Echols), 1465 (census 'previous', and Ace's table per Echols), 1476 (census and Wikipedia), 1480 (minortriad, undated).

summary: Sources read: the census preprint arXiv 2607.15270 in its v1, v2 and v3 HTML (the PDF was binary to my tools, so the text was read through a summarising fetch and quotes should be checked against the source); Taylor's arXiv 2609.27483 (HTML v1; PDF binary); the author's repository for Taylor (github.com/tommyet/snakes, file listing and README, verifier not run); Ace's four Zenodo records (17344872, 17538015, 17832883 v3, 20753867 v1 and v2); the two Echols blog posts; the Wikipedia article and OEIS A099155; the undated minortriad.com table; and the abstracts of Wynn 2012, Allison-Paulusma 2016, QUBO 2024, and the bidirectional-search paper of June 2026. Everything else (Casella-Potter, Carlson-Hougen, Kinny, Östergård-Pettersson, Hood et al., Meyerson, Abbott-Katchalski, Zémor, Huang, the IEEE QCE version, Bernatonis, Itty) is recorded from search summaries or citations and is marked as not opened. Nothing in the window settles any a(n) for n of 9 or more. Dimension 9 is still open in the census, Wikipedia and explainxkcd. The window's lower-bound activity is: Ace's four records (Oct 2025 to Aug 2026, n = 10 to 13, superseded by his own later versions); the census (July 2026, n = 9 to 13, with the 191 snake in Q9 the headline); the Echols blog (June to July 2026, n = 12, 13 and coils); Taylor (September 2026, n = 13 to 20 and an asymptotic bound for d of 21 or more); plus a QUBO reformulation (September 2024, known values only) and a bidirectional-search method paper (June 2026, no new lengths). The n = 13 values conflict across sources (see disputes), and I could not pin the 2932 and 2934 claims to a primary source. AI involvement is in two papers. In the census, v1 and v2 contain no learned component and no AI-use statement (the 'AI' in its acknowledgements is 'the AMD University Program's AI & HPC Cluster', a compute cluster). v3 (30 September 2026, retitled 'New Snake-in-the-Box Records via Snakepit Surgery and Learned Construction') adds Beam Anchor, a graph-neural-network policy trained by the authors. Its length-190 snakes are reported as all already in the authors' annealer bank, and no record is credited to it. v3 also says the authors used 'large language models' for writing and for code, unnamed. In Taylor, the author writes: 'An LLM coding assistant (OpenAI's Astra) supported the search and programming under the author's direction.' Judgement calls I made, each open to change: (1) I listed Beam Anchor under ai.systems, because it is a trained model that generates candidate snakes, but I did not list the census's unnamed LLM use or Taylor's Astra, because both describe writing and running code, which §5.4 treats as support, not contribution. Astra is recorded verbatim, as the source names it. Press coverage I saw in search (not opened) describes Astra as an unreleased, internal model and does not mention snakes. (2) I dated the census to 16 July 2026, the v1 posting that carried the records, under the first-public-argument rule. Its AI content is from v3 (30 September 2026) and I say so in the event. (3) Classical evolutionary and Monte-Carlo searches before 2024 (Casella-Potter, Carlson-Hougen, Kinny, Meyerson) are recorded with none_found true, because they are not AI systems in this record's sense. A reader who counts evolutionary search as AI should change those. (4) The 8 July 2026 Echols post is dated by its last-updated date, since its first posting date is not shown. (5) The Itty 2934 path and the Echols 2932 snake are recorded as claims cited by others and not located, with no date. Wikipedia's table is a secondary source and does not settle any of the n = 13 values.
competing_reading: The census's title ('Learned Construction'), its abstract, and its v3 LLM statement can be read as an AI-assisted step on the snake records. The search programme behind the 2026 records is partly machine-learned and was partly written with LLM help. Taylor's record (n = 13 to 20) was produced by search code that an LLM coding assistant helped write and run 'under the author's direction'. On that reading the AI-involved events are the census and Taylor, and the judging pass should count them. Against this, the census says the 191 record came from cube-surgery annealing alone. Its learned constructor's length-190 snakes are all already in the annealer's bank, and no record is credited to Beam Anchor. The LLM statements describe writing and code, not ideas. Taylor's sentence says the assistant 'supported the search and programming', which is coding support. Neither author credits a model with an idea the result turns on.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The census's per-record provenance: which code or method produced each of 191, 379, 746, 1476 and 2924, and whether LLM-written code is in the pipeline that produced them. (2) The date and content of Itty's 2934 path at n = 13, and whether it predates the census's 'previous best 2900'. (3) A primary source for Echols's 2932 snake, or confirmation that it does not exist in that form. (4) An independent run of the census repository's verifier and of Taylor's verify.py. (5) The census v1 table: whether v1 already had 2924 at n = 13, and whether v1 contained any AI content at all (v1 and v2 read as none, through a summarising fetch). (6) An author statement on which code produced Taylor's records and what the assistant wrote. (7) The Bernatonis record for n = 14 to 17. (8) The current minortriad table with a date, to settle the 2946 and 750 / 1480 values.

judgement.why: The statement asks for the exact maximum snake length in Q_n for every n; nothing in the window determines any a(n) for n >= 9, so every in-window event that improves a length is a bound (direction null), and coil/spread-k/symmetric-coil work is a variant. QUBO and the bidirectional-search paper reproduce or evaluate known values and move nothing (none). Östergård-Pettersson settles n = 8 exactly, a pre-snapshot case. The census and Taylor give explicit snakes with verifiers, so checkable. AI role: the census's Beam Anchor is credited with no record — its 190-snakes are below the 191 record and all already in the annealer's bank, and §6 credits the 191 to annealing alone — so it produced nothing that is in the result: none. The census's unnamed LLMs and Taylor's 'LLM coding assistant (OpenAI's Astra) supported the search and programming' describe coding and writing support, which is none under F12. Year-only 2026 dates and the undated Itty claim are answered null. The first Echols post shows only a last-updated date of June 2026 and is year-precision, so null.
judgement.doubts: Taylor's Astra disclosure is the closest AI call: if the search code the assistant wrote embodied the construction idea, it could be assisted, but the quote says only 'supported the search and programming under the author's direction'. The census AI reading rests on HTML read through a summarising fetch. The n = 13 values conflict across sources (2900/2924/2932/2934/2938/2946), but this does not change any scope answer.
